paragraphs: Mutual transfer learning considers several data domains without fixing which ones provide knowledge and which ones receive it. A domain can potentially play either role. This makes learning the relationships between domains part of the problem itself, alongside estimating the parameters needed for learning. The paper addresses a tension in earlier approaches: some require substantial computation, while others simplify the underlying assumptions too much.

The proposed method, DiffS, introduces a distance measure called standardized domain difference. It uses this measure to recover the learnability structure between domains while also estimating parameters accurately. The central idea is that a carefully designed comparison between domains can support both tasks, rather than making structure recovery prohibitively expensive.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the method’s effectiveness. The authors report an approximately 3,000-fold speedup over similar methods while retaining the same accuracy in estimating the learnability structure. This is an empirical comparison in the evaluated settings: its significance is the substantial computational saving achieved without sacrificing that reported structure-estimation accuracy.
icml-2022-a-difference-standardization-m.tldr: DiffS uses standardized differences between domains to recover mutual-transfer relationships accurately, with a reported roughly 3,000-fold speedup over similar methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning in episodic games where two players have opposing objectives. Most previous algorithms with efficiency guarantees for these Markov games use optimism: they favor possibilities that look promising under uncertainty. This work develops a different route through posterior sampling, bringing an approach already studied in bandits and reinforcement learning into a self-play setting with general function approximation.

The theoretical contribution depends on a new measure called the multi-agent decoupling coefficient. It characterizes a form of problem complexity relevant to the analysis. When this coefficient is low, the algorithm has a regret bound growing with the square root of the number of episodes. Thus, the guarantee is conditional on this complexity measure, rather than a claim covering every possible game equally.

For linear Markov games, the resulting regret bound matches the strongest existing results described in the abstract. The authors also identify their method as, to their knowledge, the first provably efficient posterior-sampling approach for Markov games with frequentist regret guarantees. The contribution expands the available theoretical tools for learning competitive behavior.
icml-2022-a-self-play-posterior-sampling.tldr: A self-play posterior-sampling algorithm achieves square-root regret for zero-sum Markov games with low multi-agent decoupling complexity.

paragraphs: A probability distribution can be approximated by a finite collection of points, or particles. Instead of drawing these points independently, optimization methods let them interact and move toward a better representation of the target distribution. This paper asks how accurately a limited number of such particles can represent the target, a question called quantization.

The authors analyze methods based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy and Kernel Stein Discrepancy. They prove upper bounds on quantization error with rates substantially better than those of independent random samples. They also compare different gradient flows, connecting the way particles move during optimization to the quality of the distribution approximation they ultimately provide.

Numerical experiments show fast approximation rates and improvements over greedy methods such as kernel herding. The paper additionally introduces Normalized Stein Variational Gradient Descent and argues for adaptive kernels, which exhibit faster convergence. Its comparison of Gaussian and Laplace kernels supports using the Laplace kernel for more robust quantization. Together, these results examine both theoretical approximation quality and practical choices in particle optimization.
icml-2022-accurate-quantization-of-measu.tldr: Interacting particle methods achieve strong distribution-approximation rates, with theoretical bounds outperforming independent sampling and experiments supporting adaptive and Laplace kernels.

paragraphs: Adam combines adaptive learning rates with momentum, but the two ingredients may influence training differently. This paper separates their effects within a diffusion-based theoretical framework. It focuses on escaping saddle points, where optimization can stall, and selecting flat minima, regions where nearby parameter changes have relatively little effect on the training objective.

The analysis shows that adaptive learning rates can escape saddle points efficiently but do not select flat minima in the way SGD does. Momentum instead supplies a drift that helps training pass through saddle points while having almost no effect on flat-minimum selection. The authors present this as a partial explanation for the observed contrast between Adam’s faster convergence and SGD’s often better generalization.

Motivated by this distinction, the paper proposes Adaptive Inertia, which adapts inertia separately for individual parameters. The framework accelerates training while provably favoring flat minima as SGD does. Extensive experiments report significantly better generalization than SGD and conventional adaptive gradient methods. These experimental findings complement the theoretical account of how different optimizer components affect training.
icml-2022-adaptive-inertia-disentangling.tldr: Adaptive Inertia separates adaptation from learning-rate scaling to accelerate training while preserving SGD-like preference for flat minima.

paragraphs: Weight sharing makes neural architecture search cheaper by letting candidate networks reuse trained operators. However, updates useful for one candidate can interfere with another, weakening the agreement between estimated and actual performance rankings. The paper investigates this interference by sampling candidate models and comparing the gradients they produce for shared operators.

Two observations guide the proposed fixes. Interference increases as two candidates differ in more operators, and it decreases when a shared operator receives and produces more similar representations. Accordingly, one method changes only a single operator between consecutive optimization steps. The other encourages shared operators to have similar inputs and outputs across candidate models.

Experiments in a BERT search space show that each intervention improves ranking agreement, with stronger results when combined. The discovered architecture also outperforms the reported RoBERTa and ELECTRA baselines on GLUE. Further evaluations cover BERT compression, reading comprehension, and large-scale image classification. These findings support treating interference as a practical obstacle to reliable architecture selection and show benefits from explicitly reducing it.
icml-2022-analyzing-and-mitigating-inter.tldr: Reducing interference between networks that share weights improves architecture rankings and the performance of architectures selected through search.

paragraphs: A useful representation of a scene should support separating its objects and combining them in different arrangements. Existing objectness metrics often assess pixel masks and assume that a generative model assigns objects to dedicated slots. That requirement restricts which models can be evaluated, even when other representations might contain meaningful object structure.

COAT, the Compositional Object Algebra Test, moves the evaluation into representation space. It checks geometric properties that support object composition in a generic representation. The intended distinction is between compositional structure learned by the model and structure already available in raw pixels. This makes the evaluation applicable to a wider class of models than methods requiring object-specific slots.

Experiments on CLEVR find that existing generative models based on disentanglement are less compositional than might be expected. Separating factors of variation therefore does not, in these experiments, deliver the anticipated degree of object composition. The authors hope COAT can support a common evaluation approach across generative, discriminative, and self-supervised representations, while exposing opportunities to improve their object structure.
icml-2022-coat-measuring-object-composit.tldr: COAT evaluates object compositionality directly in representation space, revealing weaker-than-expected composition in tested disentanglement-based generative models.

paragraphs: Distributed training can spend substantial effort communicating gradients between workers. Random block-wise sparsification reduces that traffic and fits ring-allreduce communication, but its computational convenience comes with poorer learning performance. This paper examines how to improve distributed SGD using this compressor by reconsidering the balance between gradient variance and the gradient’s second moment.

The resulting algorithm, detached error feedback, or DEF, has a better convergence bound than error feedback for non-convex problems. The authors also introduce DEF-A to improve generalization early in training. Their analysis gives DEF-A better generalization bounds than DEF, distinguishing the basic method’s convergence contribution from the accelerated variant’s generalization contribution.

The paper further establishes a connection between communication-efficient distributed SGD and SGD with iterate averaging. This relates compressed distributed training to another way of organizing the optimization process. Extensive deep learning experiments show substantial empirical improvements across multiple settings. The contribution therefore combines improved theoretical bounds, a conceptual connection to averaging, and practical evidence that the proposed corrections help training under gradient compression.
icml-2022-detached-error-feedback-for-di.tldr: Detached error feedback improves theoretical and empirical behavior of distributed SGD with random block sparsification, with a variant targeting early generalization.

paragraphs: Explaining a graph neural network can require understanding how features interact, rather than assigning importance to each feature independently. GNN-LRP addresses such interactions by attributing relevance to walks through nodes across network layers. However, obtaining a subgraph’s attribution appears to require adding contributions from exponentially many walks, making direct computation expensive as depth grows.

The paper shows that this exponential enumeration can be avoided. Its algorithms use message passing and the distributive property to combine the required quantities directly. This produces GNN-LRP subgraph attributions in time that grows linearly with network depth. The stated complexity improvement concerns depth specifically, rather than asserting linear cost in every aspect of the graph or model.

The authors also extend the algorithms to a generalized attribution that includes neighboring graph features. This allows explanations to account for context around the subgraph being assessed. Experiments report substantial acceleration and demonstrate the usefulness and scalability of the generalized method. The main advance makes interaction-based explanations more computationally accessible without requiring explicit enumeration of all contributing walks.
icml-2022-efficient-computation-of-highe.tldr: Message-passing algorithms compute GNN-LRP subgraph attributions in time linear in network depth and extend them to include neighboring features.

paragraphs: Standard attention becomes expensive as the number of tokens increases because its computational cost grows quadratically. Previous linear-time approaches can need added assumptions, such as favoring nearby tokens, to keep attention from collapsing into an uninformative distribution. Flowformer seeks efficient attention without imposing those particular biases, preserving flexibility across different kinds of data.

The paper interprets attention as a flow network. Values supply information, output representations receive it, and learned attention determines the capacities connecting them. Flow-Attention imposes conservation constraints on this flow: conserving incoming flow at outputs creates competition among sources, while conserving outgoing flow from sources governs allocation to outputs. These constraints generate informative attention within a mechanism of linear complexity.

The resulting Flowformer is reported to perform strongly across long sequences, time series, vision, language, and reinforcement learning. The breadth of these evaluations matters because the mechanism is designed to avoid assumptions tied to a particular application. The central contribution is a conservation-based way to structure efficient attention, together with empirical evidence of usefulness across several domains.
icml-2022-flowformer-linearizing-transfo.tldr: Flowformer uses conservation constraints on information flow to create linear-complexity attention without specific inductive biases such as locality.

paragraphs: Observed measurements may be generated by hidden variables that themselves influence one another. Discovering relationships only among the measurements can therefore leave the underlying causal organization unresolved. This paper studies recovering hidden causal variables together with the relationships among them and the connections from hidden variables to measured ones.

The framework allows a hidden variable to have other hidden variables as children, relaxing a commonly used measurement assumption. The authors define a particular minimal latent hierarchical structure. For linear, non-Gaussian models with that structure, they prove that the entire structure is identifiable using only measured variables. The result is tied to these model and structural conditions, rather than applying to arbitrary hidden causal systems.

To turn the identification result into a method, the paper tests Generalized Independent Noise conditions in specific ways. These tests provide the basis for reconstructing the hidden hierarchy. Experiments with synthetic and real-world data support the approach’s effectiveness. Its significance is that, under the stated conditions, observed data can reveal causal organization extending beyond the variables directly measured.
icml-2022-identification-of-linear-non-g.tldr: Under linear, non-Gaussian and minimal-hierarchy conditions, the paper identifies hidden causal structure from measured variables using Generalized Independent Noise tests.

paragraphs: Bayesian updating changes prior information after observing data. This paper represents that information through expected features: it updates prior feature averages into posterior feature averages. Regression from kernel features or neural-network features of observations supplies the update. All quantities used in this computation are learned from observed data, making the proposed procedure model-free in the sense stated by the authors.

The method is a new form of kernel Bayes’ rule based on importance weighting. This choice improves numerical stability relative to an existing kernel Bayes’ rule approach that requires operator inversion. The authors also prove convergence of the estimator through a new consistency analysis of the importance-weighting estimator in the infinity norm.

Evaluations use challenging synthetic benchmarks, including filtering in a state-space model whose observations are high-dimensional images. Across those experiments, the proposed method consistently outperforms the existing kernel Bayes’ rule and is competitive with other methods. The paper’s contribution combines a more stable way to perform feature-based Bayesian updates with a convergence result and empirical evidence on demanding observation spaces.
icml-2022-importance-weighted-kernel-bay.tldr: Importance weighting yields a more numerically stable kernel Bayes’ rule, with estimator convergence and improved performance on the evaluated synthetic benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether two observed continuous variables can be distinguished as cause and effect using samples of their joint distribution. Its focus is heteroscedastic noise: the amount of unexplained variation can change with the value of the cause. Accounting for that changing variation is central to the proposed approach to causal direction.

The method divides the candidate cause’s domain into segments and chooses the partition by minimizing a scale-invariant, penalized regression score. Dynamic programming finds the optimal partition for this objective. This makes segmentation part of the fitted model, allowing the procedure to accommodate noise whose behavior varies across the cause’s domain.

The authors establish conditions for identifying direction in linear models with heteroscedastic noise and nonlinear models with constant noise variance. For the setting combining nonlinearity and heteroscedasticity, support is empirical. Across synthetic and real-world datasets, modeling changing noise variance improves the ability to tell cause from effect. The distinction between the proved settings and the empirically supported extension is central to understanding the result’s scope.
icml-2022-inferring-cause-and-effect-in-.tldr: A partitioned regression method improves causal-direction inference by modeling changing noise variance, with identification results in specified settings and broader empirical support.

paragraphs: A common training procedure runs SGD with an initially constant learning rate, reduces it geometrically in stages, and returns the final parameter estimate. Although this procedure is well understood for classical linear regression, its final output had lacked a sharp analysis in overparameterized settings. This paper studies that final output directly through problem-dependent excess-risk bounds.

For a schedule with geometric decay in its later stages, the authors prove upper and lower bounds that nearly match. Upper bounds describe how large the excess risk can be, while lower bounds establish how far such guarantees can be improved. Their close agreement gives a sharper characterization of the final iterate’s statistical performance for the regression problems considered.

The paper also derives an excess-risk lower bound for polynomially decaying learning rates. This supports an instance-wise advantage for geometric decay, complementing earlier comparisons based on worst-case minimax rates. The distinction matters because a problem-dependent analysis examines how schedules behave for particular regression instances, adding detail beyond a single worst-case assessment across a problem class.
icml-2022-last-iterate-risk-bounds-of-sg.tldr: Nearly matching risk bounds characterize final-iterate SGD with geometric learning-rate decay in overparameterized linear regression and support instance-wise advantages over polynomial decay.

paragraphs: Voice-separation systems commonly assume a known or fixed maximum number of speakers and learn from supervised mixtures built with generic conditions. This paper changes the target to relax both constraints. Instead of requiring an individual output for every voice, it separates mixtures by conical regions around the listener’s head. A region may therefore still contain multiple speakers.

The proposed two-stage framework learns from overheard voices captured through earphones. First, it extracts relatively clean signals personalized to the listener. It then uses those signals to train a model for separating sound by region. This process aims to learn fine spatial distinctions, including the sound distortions introduced by the individual’s head shape.

Results are described as promising and emphasize the value of personalization compared with a generic supervised approach. The change in task definition is consequential: spatial separation can remain useful when there are too many voices to isolate individually. The authors suggest potential applications in selective hearing, noise cancellation, and audio augmented reality, presenting those uses as possibilities rather than established deployment outcomes.
icml-2022-learning-to-separate-voices-by.tldr: A personalized self-supervised system separates voices by spatial region, relaxing fixed-speaker-count assumptions by allowing each output to contain a regional mixture.

paragraphs: Policy optimization directly improves an agent’s behavior, but its theoretical guarantees have lagged behind the best achievable learning rates. This paper examines episodic tabular reinforcement learning, where states and actions are explicitly enumerated and behavior can vary within an episode. It introduces Reference-based Policy Optimization with Stable at Any Time guarantee, or RPO-SAT, to narrow that gap.

The authors prove a regret bound of approximately √(SAH³K) + √(AH⁴K), suppressing logarithmic factors. Here S counts states, A counts actions, H is episode length, and K counts episodes. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to optimal behavior. The first term matches the information-theoretic lower-bound scaling stated in the abstract, while the second contributes an additional cost.

When the number of states exceeds the episode length, the algorithm is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. That condition is part of the optimality claim. The authors describe RPO-SAT as, to their knowledge, the first computationally efficient policy-based algorithm that is nearly minimax optimal for tabular reinforcement learning, strengthening the theoretical case for this widely used algorithm family.
icml-2022-nearly-optimal-policy-optimiza.tldr: RPO-SAT gives nearly optimal policy-optimization regret in tabular reinforcement learning, achieving minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors when states outnumber the horizon.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning chooses which tasks to learn from during training, but explaining its statistical benefits requires separating a good curriculum from the effort needed to discover one. This paper makes that distinction in multitask linear regression. It considers both structured and unstructured settings and compares an optimal curriculum supplied by an oracle with one learned adaptively by the agent.

For each setting, the authors derive minimax rates, which characterize the best achievable worst-case statistical performance. Their results show that discovering a curriculum can be fundamentally harder than receiving the optimal one in the unstructured setting. In the structured setting, adaptive discovery introduces only a small additional term. Thus, the cost of learning how to allocate training depends substantially on the setting’s structure.

The paper also studies a practical rule that selects tasks with the largest local prediction gain. By comparing its guarantees with the derived minimax rates, the authors provide theoretical justification for this empirical strategy. The contribution connects the potential value of an ideal curriculum with the feasibility of finding a useful one during learning.
icml-2022-on-the-statistical-benefits-of.tldr: In multitask linear regression, discovering a curriculum can be costly without structure but adds only a small statistical penalty in the structured setting.

paragraphs: The paper studies clustering when an algorithm can ask whether two items belong together, but the answers are unreliable. Each answer is correct with probability 1/2 + δ/2, so δ measures how informative the oracle is beyond guessing. The aim is to recover k hidden clusters among n items using as few queries as possible.

Using a connection to multi-armed bandits, the authors develop a polynomial-time algorithm whose main query cost is n(k + log n)/δ², plus an additional polynomial term. Earlier upper bounds had a main term proportional to nk log n/δ². The new expression replaces the multiplication of k and log n with their sum, reducing the leading query requirement.

The authors also prove that n log n/δ² queries are necessary. Combined with an existing nk/δ² lower bound, this matches the new upper bound up to the additive polynomial term, yielding matching results over a broad parameter range. The bandit connection is therefore useful both algorithmically and for clarifying how much information noisy clustering inherently requires.
icml-2022-optimal-clustering-with-noisy-.tldr: A bandit-based clustering algorithm reduces noisy-query requirements and matches combined lower bounds up to an additive polynomial term.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning pulls related representations together and pushes designated negatives apart. Highly similar negatives can be useful training examples, but this paper finds limited benefits from importing existing hard-negative selection methods into graph learning. Its experimental and theoretical analysis attributes the problem to message passing in graph neural networks.

When candidates are selected only by similarity, many hard negatives may actually belong to the same class as the anchor. Pushing them away would then separate examples that should remain related. ProGCL estimates the probability that a candidate is a true negative and combines that estimate with similarity to judge hardness. The paper develops two associated schemes, ProGCL-weight and ProGCL-mix.

Experiments show consistent improvements over base graph contrastive methods, multiple leading results on unsupervised benchmarks, and performance exceeding supervised methods in some cases. The approach can also be inserted into various graph contrastive methods that use negatives. Its main lesson is that similarity alone can be misleading: selecting useful difficult examples also requires considering whether the negative assignment is plausible.
icml-2022-progcl-rethinking-hard-negativ.tldr: ProGCL improves graph contrastive learning by judging hard negatives using both similarity and the estimated probability that they are truly negative.

paragraphs: Learning a new control task from a few demonstrations requires extracting useful task information quickly. This paper investigates how architecture can support that ability in offline reinforcement learning. Its Prompt-based Decision Transformer, or Prompt-DT, combines a Transformer’s sequence-modeling capability with prompts that describe the task through examples of behavior.

The prompt consists of short segments from the available demonstration trajectories. Those segments encode task-specific information and guide the policy generated by the model. Adaptation therefore occurs by supplying a trajectory prompt, with the reported evaluations requiring no additional fine-tuning on unseen target tasks. The design makes demonstration context a direct input to policy generation.

Across five MuJoCo control benchmarks, Prompt-DT substantially outperforms its variants and strong offline meta-reinforcement-learning baselines using prompts containing only a few timesteps. The experiments also report robustness to changes in prompt length and generalization to out-of-distribution environments. These findings support trajectory prompting as an effective architectural route to few-shot policy adaptation in the evaluated settings.
icml-2022-prompting-decision-transformer.tldr: Prompt-DT uses short demonstration trajectories to guide policies for unseen tasks, achieving strong few-shot control results without additional fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Image retrieval systems can return problematic matches after small adversarial changes to a query image. RetrievalGuard targets the top retrieved result, seeking to keep Recall@1 unchanged under bounded perturbations. The paper develops a one-nearest-neighbor retrieval algorithm with a calculable robustness radius measured using the ℓ₂ norm.

Starting from a base retrieval model and a query, the method constructs a smoothed retrieval model. Its analysis explicitly accounts for nearest-neighbor search in a high-dimensional embedding space. The authors show that the smoothed model has a bounded Lipschitz constant, controlling how sensitively it can respond to input changes, and use the analysis to establish the stated retrieval-score invariance.

The guarantee applies to adversarial perturbations inside the calculated ℓ₂ ball. This radius is essential to the claim: the result concerns a certified neighborhood around the query. Experiments on image retrieval tasks support the method’s robustness. The contribution combines an explicit mathematical guarantee with a construction that addresses the retrieval decision itself and the geometry of its embedding space.
icml-2022-retrievalguard-provably-robust.tldr: RetrievalGuard smooths an image retrieval model to certify Recall@1 robustness against adversarial perturbations within a calculable ℓ₂ radius.

paragraphs: An agent entering a changed environment may need to act before it can confidently identify the new conditions. System identification tries to infer those conditions from experience, while robust reinforcement learning prepares for worst-case possibilities. The paper addresses a gap between these approaches: identification may be too slow, and conventional robust training generally assumes one uncertainty set specified in advance.

The authors formulate a problem involving robustness across multiple perturbation sets. Their algorithm uses a few interactions to reduce uncertainty when the observations allow it, while maintaining robustness to the uncertainty that remains. This combines learning about the current environment with preparing for adverse possibilities that experience has not yet ruled out.

Across a diverse collection of control tasks, the approach improves worst-case performance in new environments compared with methods based on system identification alone or robust reinforcement learning alone. The findings support adapting the uncertainty description as experience arrives. The practical significance is the ability to benefit from limited identification without requiring uncertainty to disappear before acting robustly.
icml-2022-robust-policy-learning-over-mu.tldr: The proposed policy-learning method reduces uncertainty through limited interaction while remaining robust to unresolved possibilities across multiple perturbation sets.

paragraphs: Self-supervised graph learning aims to learn useful representations without labels. Many methods adapt contrastive learning, which requires generated views and enough negative examples. Predictive alternatives avoid negative sampling, but their training tasks have often lacked theoretical guidance. LaGraph addresses this design question by grounding predictive learning in the goal of recovering unobserved latent graphs.

The framework derives usable self-supervised objectives as upper bounds on objectives for latent-graph prediction. This gives the training task a connection to a stated prediction goal, even though the latent graphs themselves are unobserved. The analysis also explains recent successes of predictive methods using invariance-based objectives and compares LaGraph with related approaches from other domains.

Experiments report improved performance on both graph-level and node-level tasks, together with robustness as the number of training samples decreases. These findings support the usefulness of the derived objectives across two scales of graph prediction. The central contribution is a theoretical foundation for constructing predictive self-supervised tasks, accompanied by evidence that this foundation produces effective graph representations.
icml-2022-self-supervised-representation.tldr: LaGraph derives self-supervised objectives from latent-graph prediction, improving graph representations and showing robustness to smaller training sets in experiments.

paragraphs: SkexGen generates CAD models through construction sequences containing sketch-and-extrude operations. The generated object is therefore described through a sequence of modeling actions. The paper’s focus is on representing different kinds of variation within these sequences so that generation can produce diverse designs while giving users control over selected properties.

The model uses separate Transformer architectures to encode topological, geometric, and extrusion variations into disentangled codebooks. These codebooks provide distinct representations of the different aspects of a construction sequence. Autoregressive Transformer decoders then generate sequences whose shared properties are specified by the chosen codebook vectors. Generation proceeds sequentially, with the codebook representation guiding which properties the resulting designs share.

Extensive experiments report diverse, high-quality CAD models, improved user control, and efficient exploration of the design space. These findings support the value of separating construction properties in the learned representation. The contribution links controllable sequence generation to the structure of CAD modeling operations, allowing codebook choices to guide families of designs with specified common characteristics.
icml-2022-skexgen-autoregressive-generat.tldr: SkexGen generates controllable CAD construction sequences using separate codebooks for topology, geometry, and extrusion properties.

paragraphs: Learning in high-dimensional spaces is often expected to demand enormous amounts of data, yet modern machine learning frequently succeeds with much less. This paper studies that puzzle by treating the data distribution, model, and inference algorithm as an integrated system. Its premise is that analyzing these components separately can overlook interactions that help mitigate dimensionality’s statistical cost.

The authors examine symmetries associated with learning algorithms across four architecture types: fully connected networks, locally connected networks, and convolutional networks with and without pooling. They then consider how those symmetries align with the data distribution. This puts compatibility between the learning system and the data at the center of the analysis.

The reported finding is that learning is most efficient when the relevant symmetries are compatible. Performance deteriorates substantially when any component of the data-model-inference combination is inconsistent or suboptimal. The work therefore identifies synergy across the full learning setup as an important contributor to efficiency, offering a way to study why high-dimensional learning can work well without attributing success to architecture alone.
icml-2022-synergy-and-symmetry-in-deep-l.tldr: The paper links learning efficiency to compatible symmetries across the data, model, and inference algorithm considered as one system.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks are designed so that transformations of their inputs produce corresponding transformations of their features. This paper presents a unified Fourier-based framework for such networks on homogeneous spaces, considering tensor-valued feature fields before and after convolution. It addresses both convolutional kernels and nonlinear activations, two components that must fit the desired transformation behavior.

The kernel derivation uses sparsity in the Fourier coefficients of lifted feature fields. This sparsity arises when the space’s stabilizer subgroup is a compact Lie group. For nonlinear processing, the framework lifts features to the regular representation, applies an elementwise nonlinearity, and projects back through an equivariant convolution. The authors show that other activations using Fourier coefficients in the stabilizer subgroup are special cases.

Experiments involving SO(3) and SE(3) report state-of-the-art results in spherical vector-field regression, point-cloud classification, and molecular completion. These results accompany the framework’s unifying mathematical contribution. By deriving kernels and activations through a common perspective, the paper connects previously separate design choices and demonstrates their usefulness on several geometric learning tasks.
icml-2022-unified-fourier-based-kernel-a.tldr: A Fourier-based framework unifies equivariant convolution kernels and nonlinear activations, with strong reported results across geometric learning tasks.
